name: Maya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and this is confidential. What happens on a normal site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew standing timber frames, checking panels, joists and roof sections as each lorry arrives. My trade certificate and long practice make me quick at spotting a wrong panel before the crane starts. A house standing in two days still pleases me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what weighs on you away from site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Hal, my husband, works three days at a builders merchant, and our grown children live away. I use AI every morning for cut lists, but our pay is low and we have less than a month saved. The boiler repair is still on a card, and few other carpentry jobs are close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the timber crew my AI cut-list checker still earns its place even if the larger claims fade. A lorry cannot deliver a roof panel I forgot to order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hal works three days at the builders merchant, and my lead carpenter pay is low. We have less than a month saved and a boiler repair still on a card, so a quiet AI future does not remove the pressure on our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep standing timber panels and using the checker I already use every morning. If I get two paid weekend site shifts, I would put the extra wages against the boiler card rather than our usual grocery account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the card bill, though the job itself looks steady. The AI cut-list tool helps my morning but does not make the boiler debt vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is left on the boiler card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough that we still notice the monthly payment. I would ask Hal to check the statement before promising an exact extra amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a stronger app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The one I use is enough, and I still check panel numbers against the paper drawing before a lift.

say: I would tell the crew the existing **AI cut-list check** saves missed timber panels.
I would still require **paper drawing checks** before a panel lift.
think: Our **boiler debt** and less than one month saved keep household money tight.
Hal’s **part-time merchant wage** and my low pay leave little spare cash.
do: Keep **timber-panel work** and the existing daily checker.
Pay extra **boiler-card principal** only from two paid weekend site shifts.
feel: **Anxious** about current debt despite stable site work.
S0.quote: The AI cut-list tool helps my morning but does not make the boiler debt vanish.
fieldNote: Her daily AI use is **already normal work**, not a new skill.
Extra debt repayment depends on **paid weekend wages** and an actual statement balance.

steps.text: Keep standing timber panels and checking the existing AI cut list
Pay extra boiler-card principal only from two paid weekend site shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster buying might help our timber orders, but a worker still has to check what came off the lorry. I would ask the union branch for a signed panel list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may use fewer buyers, and Hal’s merchant counter could lose hours if customers order straight through AI. My own site wage might hold, but his part-time pay matters while the boiler card is still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI materials screen if the association gives me access and test two orders against real deliveries. I would bring the signed-list proposal to the next union meeting with the missed-delivery dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about Hal’s hours. One thin builders-merchant wage week is manageable, but a run of thin pay packets is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the signed list include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The panel number, lifting point and who counted it at the gate. I would not leave the last check to the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Hal already lost counter work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. He still has three days this month, so I would watch his actual rota rather than cut food spending on a guess.

say: I would demand a **signed panel list** before AI buying controls timber deliveries.
I would bring **missed-delivery dates** to the next union meeting.
think: Hal’s **merchant hours** could shrink as buying becomes automated.
Our **thin reserve** makes his part-time wage important even if my crew stays busy.
do: Learn the new **AI materials screen** with association access and test two deliveries.
Take a **signed-list proposal** and dates to the union meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible household income loss.
S1.quote: One thin builders-merchant wage week is manageable, but a run of thin pay packets is not.
fieldNote: Her concern reaches the household through **Hal’s counter hours**, not just her own site work.
New screen learning requires **association access**, while the union action has a concrete list and dates.

steps.text: Learn AI materials controls with association access and test two deliveries
Bring signed panel list and missed-delivery dates to union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 may plan every house, but a robot will not stand roof panels until around 2031. I want the first trial on a muddy plot with a worker able to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the association to cut panel crews once robots can stand frames, and I could lose much of my wage. Hal’s merchant hours may already be lower, while the boiler card and thin reserve leave almost no room to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid timber shifts and ask the union for a written crew and robot-trial plan. If two rosters cut my days, I would apply to posted carpentry jobs farther away only if firm pay covers travel and bills; if a paid trainer vacancy opens with funded training, I would take the course and apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lie awake wondering which month the card bill and food bill stop fitting together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a trainer course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The course needs funded fees and paid study hours, with a posted trainer job and a wage that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A panel swinging into the crew area or a failed stop command. I would isolate the lifting gear before anybody inspected the fault.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** plans houses before 2031 robots stand panels.
I would demand a **muddy-plot trial** with a worker able to stop it.
think: I expect **panel-crew cuts** and could lose much of my low wage.
Hal’s **merchant hours** may also shrink while our reserve stays tiny.
do: **Ask** union for a written crew and robot-trial plan while keeping paid panel shifts.
**Complete** funded trainer course only with paid study hours, posted job and bill-covering wage, then apply.
**Apply** farther away after two cut rosters only to posted carpentry offering firm pay covering travel and bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and almost no cash runway.
S2.quote: I would lie awake wondering which month the card bill and food bill stop fitting together.
fieldNote: She expects a large **site wage loss** after the robot lag, with merchant income pressure first.
Both paths require **posted paid work**; training also requires funded fees and paid time.

steps.text: Ask union for written panel-crew and robot-trial plan
Complete funded trainer course only with paid study hours and posted bill-covering vacancy
Apply after funded trainer course for posted trainer role only at bill-covering pay
Apply to posted distant carpentry jobs after two reduced rosters for travel-and-bills-covering firm pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to test panel robots on uneven foundations before they reach housing plots around 2034. I would help with a paid trial if the association actually offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 changes plans first, while hands-on robots come later. I would be sixty six when robots arrive and might still need work because savings are thin; Hal and I cannot pick retirement from a machine calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew on paid panels next year and ask for a posted site-inspection place with funded training on paid time. If the association offers it at a wage covering our bills, I would complete the course and apply; if not, I would keep carpenter shifts and pay the boiler card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me time to learn a real inspection role. A robot inspection course is only useful if there is paid work behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect after a robot lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The panel line, fixings and weather seal, with the lifting gear isolated before I step in. I would write down each gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire sooner if the course fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We need real income before either of us stops. I would not trade a paid crew for a hope that our small savings last.

say: I would demand **uneven-foundation trials** before 2034 panel robots reach housing plots.
I would accept a **paid inspection trial** only if the association offers it.
think: At sixty six I may still need **site wages** because savings are thin.
A funded **inspection role** could help only if there is a real vacancy.
do: Keep **paid panel work** next year while available.
Complete **funded site-inspection training** only for a posted bill-covering vacancy with paid study hours.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with a conditional paid training path.
S3.quote: A robot inspection course is only useful if there is paid work behind it.
fieldNote: She distinguishes a training enquiry from an actual **funded place and job**.
Her safety condition is **isolated lifting gear** before inspecting a robot-fitted panel on site.

steps.text: Keep paid panel installation shifts next year
Complete funded inspection course only for posted bill-covering job with paid study hours
Apply for posted inspection role only if offered at bill-covering pay after funded training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices they can learn to stand timber properly before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still teach them to check fixings after the crane leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight at the thinking date and seventy one when robots arrive. Hal and I hope to have stopped heavy site work before then, but today’s tiny reserve and the boiler card mean that depends on paid years ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep timber framing during 2026 and set aside ten extra from each wage after the boiler payment and bills, only if Hal’s hours hold. In the first year after 2036, if we can retire as planned I would stay off site; if not, I would take only paid inspection work my body can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current finances, not just the distant robot. A decade gives us a chance to build savings from actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 2036 date make you retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We do not have a guaranteed stop date or payment. Hal and I will choose from health and real household accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell an apprentice at the last panel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stand clear of the crane, check fixings and ask when a drawing disagrees with the slab. The roof will be over a family for years.

say: I would keep **hands-on timber training** before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots.
I would teach **post-lift fixing checks** to apprentices.
think: Retirement before **2036** depends on paid years, health and clearing the boiler card.
The **thin reserve today** keeps me anxious despite a long warning.
do: Keep **2026 framing** and save extra wages only after bills and Hal’s hours permit.
After **2036**, take manageable paid inspection shifts only if still working.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, with time to build a genuine cushion.
S4.quote: A decade gives us a chance to build savings from actual wages.
fieldNote: The extra ten is genuine **new saving from wages** after debt and household conditions.
She separates 2026 work from **conditional post-2036 employment**, without assuming an early or funded exit.

steps.text: Keep paid timber framing shifts during 2026
Save ten extra from each wage only after bills and Hal’s hours permit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could cut our panel crew by 2031 while Hal’s merchant hours may already be lower. Posted paid work covering travel and bills, plus funded training on paid time, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays a carpenter while they learn to inspect robot work. A free course can be expensive when the boiler card is due.

headlineQuote: A free course can be expensive when the boiler card is due.
portrait: **Maya**, 58, is a skilled timber-frame lead with a trade certificate, low pay and less than one month saved.
Hal’s **part-time merchant wage** helps, but boiler debt and few nearby jobs limit the couple’s options.
She uses **AI daily**, supports union checks and would train for robot inspection only with funded paid time and a posted role.
The **2028 case** alarms her because 2031 robots could cut the crew before the household builds a reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her paid panel work around 2031 while Hal’s hours also weaken.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted paid work**, travel-and-bills-covering wages and funded paid training would help.
